analysis.one_liner: Gives every American child a government-funded savings account, paid for by higher estate and capital gains taxes on the wealthy.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee — no vote was ever taken on creating savings accounts for every American child.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would open a federally managed savings account for every child in America, seeded with $1,000 at birth and topped up each year with up to $2,000 for children in the poorest households. When the child turns 18, the money could be used only for education, buying a home, or retirement. To pay for it, the bill would raise taxes on very large estates, limit trust-based estate avoidance, tax capital gains when someone dies or gives assets away, and raise the capital gains rate from 20% to 24.2%. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Every child born after 2019 would get a $1,000 federal deposit at birth, with yearly contributions of up to $2,000 sliding down to zero as household income rises toward 500% of the poverty line — so the largest accounts would go to children of the poorest families. Because household wealth is heavily skewed by race and inheritance, a universal account seeded and grown by the government would disproportionately lift children who would otherwise start adulthood with nothing. The accounts are managed by the government, invested in U.S. Treasury bonds, tax-free, and cannot be counted against eligibility for federal benefits.

how_it_helps.text: Every child born after 2019 would get a $1,000 federal deposit at birth, plus yearly payments on a sliding scale — up to $2,000 per year for the poorest households, phasing to zero at 500% of the poverty line.
Money could be withdrawn only at 18 and only for education, buying a home, or retirement, so it builds long-term assets rather than being spent early.
Account balances would not count against eligibility for federal benefits like student aid, so saving would not cost a family its other support.

The program is paid for by raising the estate tax (top rates of 55% and 65% above $10 million), capping the annual gift-tax exclusion for hard-to-value transfers at $50,000, taxing capital gains at death, and raising the capital gains rate to 24.2%.

analysis.who_pays: Very wealthy families: the bill raises the top estate tax rate to 65% on estates over $50 million, restores the 2009-level $3.5 million exclusion, limits grantor retained annuity trusts and grantor trusts as estate-avoidance vehicles, caps the annual gift exclusion for certain transfers at $50,000, taxes capital gains at death above a $100,000 exclusion ($1 million for farm real property), and raises the capital gains rate from 20% to 24.2%.

drawbacks.text: It is expensive: every child gets a $1,000 seed plus annual payments up to $2,000 for the poorest households, all paid from federal general revenue, which must be raised through higher estate and capital gains taxes on wealthy families.

The accounts can only be invested in 30-year government bonds, which historically earn less than stocks, so balances would grow more slowly than private savings — a trade made for safety, at a cost to the accounts' final size.
Families above the income tiers get nothing beyond the initial $1,000, and withdrawal is restricted to education, homeownership, and retirement, limiting flexibility for account holders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a public trust fund for every child that could reach roughly $50,000 for the poorest by age 18 — is large and directly targeted at the racial and class wealth gap. The costs are real: it is expensive, funded by a big increase in estate tax and a new tax on inherited stock gains that wealthy families and their estate planners would fight hard; wealthy parents would still supplement their children outside the program, so gaps would narrow but not close; and locking the money into government bonds forgoes higher returns (and greater complexity) that private investing could offer. On balance it is a coherent, well-designed transfer program, but it never received any committee or floor action, so none of its effects ever occurred.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 23, 2019 and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
That was the only action ever taken: no subcommittee or committee vote, no floor vote, and no companion action in the Senate occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy families who would have paid the higher estate and capital gains taxes, since the bill died without ever getting a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy families who would have paid the new taxes

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, letting it die in committee without any recorded action.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans supported the bill, and the Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill pays for children's accounts by raising the estate tax to 65% above $50 million, limiting GRATs and grantor trusts, taxing capital gains at death, and lifting the top capital gains rate to 24.2% — a direct hit to the families and advisers who use these vehicles.
Children's savings would sit in a government fund invested in Treasury bonds rather than in private brokerage accounts, keeping those assets away from the financial industry.
Restrictions on grantor trusts and a $50,000 annual cap on excluded gifts to trusts would close off common techniques for passing large estates tax-free.
